articles.title_orig: US death row inmate survives execution attempt after two lethal injections
articles.title_zh: US death row inmate survives execution attempt after two lethal injections
articles.content_orig:
What we know after Christa Pike survived two lethal injections
Tennessee death row inmate Christa Pike has been taken to hospital after an attempt to execute her by two lethal injections failed, her lawyer says.
Her legal team filed an emergency motion to halt the convicted murderer's execution as it was happening, saying: "Ms Pike has lost consciousness and still has a heartbeat and is audibly snoring."
One of her attorneys told the BBC that Pike, 50, was now "being provided life-saving measures" in hospital after two syringes of pentobarbital had been administered.
Pike was sentenced to death in 1996 for the murder of 19-year-old Colleen Slemmer. Her execution was the subject of a last-minute legal battle.
This culminated in the US Supreme Court allowing the lethal injections to go ahead.
Pike was 18 when she and her then-boyfriend, Tadaryl Shipp, beat, tortured and killed 19-year-old Slemmer, whom they had met at a job training camp for troubled teens.
Slemmer's mother May Martinez was among those who wanted the execution to take place. Speaking to NBC News after Wednesday evening's events, she said: "It was a mess."
The attempted execution took place at Riverbend Maximum Security Institution in Nashville at about 20:00 local time (01:00 GMT on Thursday).
Pike was given two doses of the chemical pentobarbital, and the curtain in the witness room was closed twice, the AP news agency reported.
Media were at some point asked to leave, the news agency said.
AP added that Tennessee's execution protocol calls for a secondary set of drug syringes in case the person being put to death does not die after the first set. But it does not spell out what happens if the subject is alive after the second set.
Why there was a surge of US executions in 2025
LISTEN: Could the US death penalty ever die out?
In a statement reported by US media, Tennessee Governor Bill Lee said he had ordered "a comprehensive, third-party review to determine exactly what occurred". He said the year's last remaining execution would not go ahead as planned.
The attempted execution of Pike was not the first in the state in 2026 that did not unfold as planned. The execution of Tony Carruthers, who was convicted of kidnapping and murdering three people in 1994, was postponed in May after staff were unable to find a vein to administer a lethal drug.
The Tennessee Department of Correction has said it stands by all the actions it took during the attempted execution of Pike.
"The Tennessee Department of Correction followed every step of the State's lawful, established execution protocol approved by the Attorney General's Office," department spokesperson Dorinda Carter told the Tennessean newspaper.
"The lethal injection chemical in the protocol has consistently been effective, and the protocol does not allow for additional procedures beyond what was carried out this evening. Christa Pike has been transported to an off-site medical facility," she said.
Colleen Slemmer was tortured and brutally killed in the 1995 murder
Pike's legal team said in a statement to the Tennessean newspaper: "Tonight the State of Tennessee once again failed to carry out a lawful execution.
"We take no pleasure in being right, but the concerns raised by Ms Pike proved to be true: difficult vein access, blown veins, degraded pentobarbital, no emergency medical care available when things inevitably go wrong, all under a protocol that remains veiled in secrecy."
Pike's lawyers filed an emergency motion to stay her execution and provide medical care after the lethal injection was apparently botched.
District Judge Clifton L Corker issued a ruling noting that "medical personnel have begun to administer medical care as requested in the motion".
Dr Joel Zivot, a professor at the Emory University School of Medicine who told the BBC he had been retained by Pike's legal team as a medical expert, said she likely never achieved a sufficient blood level of pentobarbital to cause apnoea and cardiovascular failure during the attempted execution.
"It's very possible that as a consequence of the delay of the beginning of resuscitation she will have a brain injury," Zivot said in an email.
The attempted capital punishment went ahead after multiple last-minute legal challenges by Pike's lawyers failed.
The US Supreme Court had thwarted two separate efforts to stop the lethal injection.
Late on Wednesday, America's highest court overturned a reprieve granted by a lower court earlier in the day. The lower court had granted a pause, saying it needed more time to consider the arguments in Pike's case.
The Supreme Court had previously dismissed an appeal by Pike's lawyers, who had argued the jury did not get the chance to weigh mitigating evidence of Pike's documented history of childhood sexual abuse, before they sentenced her to death in 1996.
The defence said that for years, the state of Tennessee had argued in court that she lied about being sexually abused as a child.
But at a recent hearing about her execution method, the state said it did not dispute that she had suffered sexual abuse and rape.
Tennessee's governor denied a clemency request this week from Pike, the only woman on the state's death row.
May Martinez, mother of Colleen Slemmer, outside a court hearing in 2006
In her clemency petition, Pike said that she intended to beat Slemmer, not kill her, but that she was unable to "put the brakes on".
"I was a mentally ill 18-year-old kid," she said in a statement. "It took me numerous years to even realise the gravity of what I'd done. Even more to accept how many lives I affected. I took the life of someone's child, sister, friend. It sickens me now to think I had the ability to commit such a crime."
The murder in 1995 created a media frenzy in Knoxville, Tennessee, after Colleen was found with an inverted pentagram - a symbol that is associated with satanic groups - carved into her chest. Pike has denied carving the symbol herself.
Before the killing, Pike had accused Colleen of insulting her and trying to steal her then-boyfriend.
Two other residents at the camp later testified that Pike had bragged about the murder before and after, and showed them a piece of Colleen's skull.
Pike's boyfriend and co-defendant Shipp was 17 at the time so spared the death penalty under state law. He remains in prison.
Martinez, Slemmer's mother, said at the weekend that she had waited decades to see Pike's sentence carried out.
She told AP that a group helped raise funds for her and her husband to travel from Florida to Tennessee to witness the execution.
"Not a day goes by, or a minute goes by that I do not think about Colleen. Holidays are the worst," Martinez said.
Since 1976, when the Supreme Court resumed the death penalty, only 18 women have been executed in the US, compared to 1,663 men. That is about 1% of all US executions.

articles.title_orig: Trump threatens to 'blow up' Iran as talks stall
articles.title_zh: Trump threatens to 'blow up' Iran as talks stall
articles.content_orig:
US President Donald Trump said Tuesday that Iran would eventually give up, although he stopped short of predicting when, during remarks at a White House event attended by leading technology executives.
Asked whether Iran was about to concede, Trump replied: "Well, they're doing very poorly. I don't know if they're going to give up yet, but they'll give up, but they're doing very poorly."
He also claimed that more oil had moved through the Strait of Hormuz over the preceding two days than at any previous point in history, including before the war.
Trump made the remarks following a luncheon for tech leaders and artificial intelligence (AI) moguls held in the White House's East Room.
The US president did not provide figures to substantiate the claim. He reiterated that preventing Iran from acquiring a nuclear weapon remained the central objective of the military campaign.
"Iran will not have a nuclear," he said, ending the sentence without completing the phrase.
The remarks came during an event largely devoted to artificial intelligence , which Trump wants to rename "superintelligence," or SI.
Trump returned to the nuclear issue when a reporter asked why North Korea had been allowed to develop nuclear weapons while the United States was determined to prevent Iran from obtaining them.
"Ah, that's interesting. You know why? Because you had a different president, and they could have stopped him," Trump replied, blaming his predecessors for failing to halt Pyongyang's nuclear program.
He then spoke about his personal relationship with North Korean leader Kim Jong Un.
"He happens to be a friend of mine, Kim Jong Un. He's a friend of mine. He likes Trump. Doesn't like a lot of other people," Trump said.
"I'm about the only person in the entire world that he likes, and I like him. I get in a lot of heat when I say that."
Trump acknowledged that North Korea possesses a substantial nuclear capability.
"He does have a nuclear capacity, a large nuclear, pretty large nuclear. Not like us, but he has a nuclear capacity," he said.
He again contrasted the situation with his approach to Iran, saying previous presidents "didn't do what I did."
The president also addressed an investigation near RAF Fairford, a British airbase used by US forces, including for operations involving Iran.
Trump said American authorities had been involved in the investigation and criticized the decision to release five arrested men on bail.
"How do you give bail to a terrorist?" he asked, referring to the suspects.
"They put them out on bail. I assume they have them watched closely. But these were serious people, seriously bad people, and they should not have done that."
British counterterrorism police said Tuesday that no improvised explosive devices had been found during the investigation, although petrol had been recovered from vehicles. The five men remain under investigation following their release on bail. Police have said the decision was made as part of their investigative strategy.
Authorities are examining several possible explanations for the incident, including whether individuals may have been acting on behalf of a foreign state. An Iranian connection has not been established, and Iran has denied involvement.
Trump said his recent meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping had been discussed with the technology executives gathered at the White House.
"We had a great meeting with President Xi. A lot of respect for President Xi," he said.
The discussion then turned to competition between the United States and China over AI infrastructure.
Trump argued that American companies must be able to build data centers domestically rather than move projects overseas.
"If we're not smart, they'll end up building data centers in other countries, and those other countries will make a fortune, and we won't," he said.
He suggested that China would welcome American investment that failed to materialize in the United States.
"Elon and I sat with President Xi the other day, and he will take every data center that we don't want," Trump said, referring to Elon Musk.
Trump also praised the American technology industry's position in the global AI race.
"Our companies are dominating the world," he said. "They're dominating China. They're dominating everyone. We want to keep it that way."
The White House said following Xi's recent visit that the two countries had agreed to use the term "superintelligence" and establish a dialogue on the technology's risks and benefits.
Musk was asked what superintelligence could mean for workers concerned that their jobs may disappear.
"I think by far the most likely outcome is an age of abundance, where we don't have just universal basic income. We have universal high income," he said.
Musk argued that advances in robotics and superintelligence could eventually make medical care far more widely available.
Pressed on what people would do without jobs, he said: "Well, jobs are going to change. Jobs have always changed."
He compared the potential transition to the disappearance of jobs once devoted to performing calculations by hand, work that is now done by computers.
Not every executive offered an unqualifiedly optimistic view.
Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei emphasized that AI presents significant risks alongside its benefits.
"I think the technology has very real risks, and you know, the mechanism by which we address those risks is still under discussion," he said.
Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg described an agreement among industry leaders on internal controls, outside audits and independent reviews by company boards. He characterized the commitments as an initial step rather than a complete solution.
Trump, meanwhile, expressed confidence that the companies had strong incentives to ensure their products were safe.
"If something goes wrong, their companies are at stake," he said. "They're not going to let that happen."
The exchanges illustrated how an event intended to promote America's technological ambitions became a forum for questions extending from AI safety and competition with China to the Iran war and security concerns in Britain.

articles.title_orig: Trump’s Latest Attempt to Cheat in the Midterms Faces Little Blowback
articles.title_zh: Trump’s Latest Attempt to Cheat in the Midterms Faces Little Blowback
articles.content_orig:
This is Executive Dysfunction , a newsletter that highlights one under-the-radar story about how Trump is changing the law—or how the law is pushing back—and keeps you posted on the latest from Slate’s Jurisprudence team. Click here to receive it in your inbox each week.
Midterm elections are around the corner, and for months, while strategists have predicted a Democratic sweep, the GOP has been throwing everything and the kitchen sink at its base in hopes of mitigating the anticipated blue wave. This past week, those efforts took the form of a series of television ads, each one featuring President Donald Trump and highlighting his administration’s policies while also warning against unspecified threats of communism. The ads themselves, though, were not the most disturbing thing. The most alarming part of the ads is a small disclaimer at the bottom of the screen: “Paid for by the U.S. government.” It appears that Trump was using our taxpayer dollars to fund his midterm political efforts. Using taxpayer dollars for ads that are clearly political is a blatant violation of federal law, but the unfortunate reality is that there may not be a clear-cut way to actually stop the Trump administration from continuing to air them.
At least three ads began airing over the past week across national and local TV networks, one of them a montage of Trump as president with a voice-over of him saying, “America will never be a communist country,” and the song “Love Me” by JMSN playing. Another ad is nearly identical to one aired during Trump’s 2024 campaign for president, in which he vows to “throw off the sick political class that hates our country” and “rout the fake news media.” Of course, in 2024 that ad was paid for by campaign funds, not taxpayers. By Sunday evening, the Wall Street Journal estimated that the ads had aired nearly 90 times across national TV networks and cost about $337,000. They also ran in local TV stations, with about 2,000 airings estimated to cost $1.4 million. The Journal also reported that the ads were paid for with taxpayer dollars that Congress appropriated to Homeland Security for Customs and Border Protection, an agency that regularly runs ads about immigration policies. Indeed, former DHS Secretary Kristi Noem was fired after she spent $220 million on an ad blitz featuring her on a horse in front of Mount Rushmore.
The White House has insisted these ads are merely public service announcements “reminding Americans to love their country and understand what makes it worth defending, at home, at our borders, and abroad.” However, it’s obvious that these are not PSAs, as they do not attempt to inform anyone of new or relevant information. Not a single mention of a government program that Americans can participate in or a message about a new government policy. No one is featured in these ads besides Trump. Instead, each one simply glorifies Trump, hailing him as a majestic leader of the free world, something no U.S. president has ever done before. And rightfully so, as the ads state they are paid for by the U.S. government, an explicit violation of the Antideficiency Act and the Hatch Act too.
Nearly all appropriations bills that Congress passes include a rider that says none of the money being awarded can be used for publicity or propaganda purposes. The Office of Legal Counsel and the Government Accountability Office have affirmed this, establishing that messages designed to self-aggrandize or extol a government official, or ones that are purely partisan in nature, are not measures that provide the public with information about government programs. “These are ads that are really designed to aggrandize the president, as indeed the ‘Love Me’ song indicates. It’s really about promoting or aggrandizing him as an individual,” Richard Briffault, professor of legislation at Columbia Law School, told me. “Not government programs, and that certainly violates the appropriations riders against publicity or propaganda.”
There are a few actions Congress can take to hold the Trump administration accountable for cutting and airing these ads. The Antideficiency Act prohibits the spending of money beyond what Congress has appropriated it for, and if in fact the White House used DHS funding to produce and distribute the Trump ads, Briffault believes, DHS’s budget “has to be cut” by the equivalent amount spent on the ads. And if Democrats are successful in clawing back a majority in Congress, they could pass a resolution to demand that DHS return the money it spent on the ads and hold public hearings about what went on behind the scenes in deciding to produce the ads and use taxpayer dollars to fund them.
Another option, something Briffault admits is petty but has been done before, is to slash the salaries of people at the agency responsible for the unlawful behavior, or even folks who worked on it.
There may also be potential Hatch Act violations in the making of the ads; the act bans political activity by federal employees, but, critically, U.S. presidents and vice presidents themselves are exempt from it. White House employees who worked on any part of the ads could be held in violation of the act, but the only way to find out would be for Congress or the Justice Department to initiate an investigation. However, under Attorney General Todd Blanche, it is nearly certain that the DOJ will not look into the lawfulness of Trump’s TV ads, putting the onus on Congress to think about how it can enforce our nation’s laws. But all of this is uncharted territory for Congress, as Briffault explained: “The problem is, the laws have never been significantly enforced because they’ve never been violated in such an egregious way,” he said.
Unfortunately, federal law does not recognize taxpayers’ standing, so average Americans can’t bring a lawsuit against the Trump ads. On Wednesday, Public Citizen, a progressive consumer rights group, filed a complaint to the Federal Communications Commission and the Federal Trade Commission demanding that the ads be pulled from the airwaves, as they appear to violate federal law. However, given that the heads of these agencies are Trump appointees, Briffault is skeptical they will oblige. Individual broadcasters could choose to not air the ads because of their illegality, but the FCC could come after them for not running them.
We hope you learned a thing or two from this edition of Executive Dysfunction. If you enjoyed reading it, please consider supporting our legal journalism by becoming a Slate Plus member !
In this week’s episode of Amicus , Dahlia Lithwick discusses Trump’s White House ban on CNN, Politico, and MS NOW with Jameel Jaffer of the Knight First Amendment Institute. They weigh the First Amendment and due process rights at stake and why the administration’s national security argument failed to hold up in court.
In the Amicus bonus episode , Dahlia and Madiba K. Dennie of Balls & Strikes unpack more lawless behavior by Immigration and Customs Enforcement and how it can directly be traced to the U.S. Supreme Court. They also discuss the recent developments over Missouri’s congressional maps and how the Trump administration is continuing to send people to third countries as a means of removing them from the U.S. as quickly as possible.
Friend of Slate Jay Willis, the editor in chief of Balls & Strikes, writes about the devolution of SCOTUSblog , the go-to outlet for Supreme Court news for nearly a quarter century. The once indispensable resource started to pivot when one of its founders was charged with tax evasion, and last year the outlet was sold to the Dispatch, a company with a conservative tilt.
SCOTUS will begin a new term in October, and Suncor v. Boulder County is expected to deliver a landmark win to the oil industry. James Goodwin and Daniel Walters write in Slate that this case landed a sympathetic audience with the current bench of Supreme Court justices who have demonstrated a pro-fossil-fuel bias.

articles.title_orig: Pakistan launches deadly airstrikes on Afghanistan
articles.title_zh: Pakistan launches deadly airstrikes on Afghanistan
articles.content_orig:
Pakistan launched airstrikes overnight on two provinces in neighboring Afghanistan , the two countries said Thursday.
The Taliban government in Kabul said at least nine civilians, all women and children, were killed, while 11 others were wounded.
Pakistani authorities, on the other hand, said the strikes had killed 22 militants. Neither casualty toll could be independently verified.
The airstrikes are the latest clash between the two neighbors since cross-border tensions spiked earlier this year .
The Afghan government spokesman said three civilian homes in the southern province of Helmand and in the eastern province of Kunar, which borders Pakistan, were hit, killing nine and injuring 11 others.
Residents of Helmand told the AFP news agency that three bombs had struck their village, and there is "no military or anything else" in the area.
"We condemn this act and consider this an act of aggression and a crime that violates all universally accepted principles," Zabihullah Mujahid said.
Authorities in Islamabad, however, said that 22 militants had been killed, and that weapons and ammunition had been destroyed.
The airstrikes on militant hideouts were "well planned and calibrated" and were carried out "with precision and accuracy," Pakistan's Ministry of Information said.
"Maximum precautions were taken and it was ensured that no collateral damage occurs," the statement said.
The strikes overnight are the third time in the past two weeks that Pakistan has hit targets in Afghanistan.
Simmering tensions since the Taliban seized power in 2021 erupted into open conflict last year ​​​​​​.
The two countries held peace talks in April to shore up a March truce , but sporadic flare-ups have continued in the months since.
Islamabad accuses the Taliban government in Kabul of harboring militants who carry out attacks across the border in Pakistan, an allegation Afghanistan denies.
"The threat to Pakistan emanates from Afghanistan," Pakistan's information ministry said. "Our action precisely targeted the terrorist hubs."
Since the conflict escalated last year , Pakistan has closed its border crossings with Afghanistan, which is heavily reliant on foreign food and humanitarian aid.
Last week, the United Nations said more than 1,100 civilians had been killed or injured in Afghanistan as a result of the cross-border conflict this year.
Pakistan insists that it does not target civilians.

articles.title_orig: Early voting data shows emerging signs of a Democratic advantage in the midterms
articles.title_zh: Early voting data shows emerging signs of a Democratic advantage in the midterms
articles.content_orig:
Election Day is still a month away, but more than 700,000 Americans have already voted across at least 30 states. There are signs emerging of the advantage Democrats have in motivating their voters – a trend that’s played out in polling all summer long.
In several states with key Senate or governor races this fall, Democrats make up a larger share of voters requesting ballots so far than they did at this point in 2024.
What early voting data is showing ahead of the 2026 midterms
In Iowa, Democrats have made 67% of ballot requests, up from 54% at this point in 2024. In Pennsylvania, it’s 66%, up from 62%, and in Maine it’s 57%, up from 53%. And according to data from the North Carolina State Board of Elections, 42% of ballot requests are from Democrats, up from 36% at this point two years ago.
It’s worth noting that in all of those states except for Iowa, ballot requests at this point in 2022 were more Democratic than they are now.
The uptick in the share of requests from Democrats would be in line with polling, special election results and primary turnout, all of which have indicated Democrats may be more motivated to vote this November.
On the other hand, it could just be further evidence of Republicans continuing to shift to preferring other forms of voting.
An important caveat: While the fact that a person has voted is generally public information, your ballot itself is secret, so this data can’t tell us how many votes a party or candidate has won. That won’t be known until states start reporting results after the polls close on November 3.
Early voting data also only shows one slice of voters: a slice that is typically older and less Republican than the electorate as a whole.
Voting patterns have shifted in the last several years as the country has emerged from the Covid-19 pandemic.
As mail voting has fallen from its 2020 highs, voters 65 and older have made up a larger share of people choosing to vote that way, going from 27% of mail voters in 2020 to 31% in 2022 and 37% in 2024, according to CNN Exit Poll data.
That’s not unexpected. Mail voting can be a convenient option for older people who might have trouble getting to the polls. In many states where voters need an excuse to vote by mail, age itself can qualify as a reason to receive a mail-in ballot.
There are early signs that that trend is continuing this year.
In nearly every state for which there is comparable data, voters 65 and older make up a larger share of ballot requests this year than they did at this point in either 2022 or 2024.
Perhaps the most positive signs for Democrats so far come from Virginia, which has reported both by far the most total votes of any state in CNN’s count and is the only state which has reported substantial numbers of both early in-person and mail votes.
While Virginia voters don’t register by party, there’s a clear relationship between how a locality voted in 2024 and its relative pace of early voting.
Cities and counties that voted for former Vice President Kamala Harris by more than 20 percentage points are at 78% of their turnout from this time in 2024, while those that voted for President Donald Trump by 20 points are at just 61%.
Partisan turnout, as measured by the share of voters who have only participated in one party’s primaries since 2022, also points to a considerable Democratic advantage in the early voting period relative to the same point in 2024.
While the turnout so far shows a clear advantage in Democratic motivation, Republican voters could close the gap as Election Day nears. It’s still early in the voting period – Virginians cast over 4.5 million votes in 2024 and over 3.4 million votes in 2025. The Senate race in Virginia is not expected to be competitive this year, and Republican voters may be more motivated in more highly contested races.
Still, two competitive House races in the state also suggest a move towards Democrats in terms of enthusiasm.
Democratic primary participants outnumber Republican primary participants by 15 points among votes cast so far in the 1st District and 18 points in the 2nd District. Both districts are battlegrounds currently represented by Republicans facing tough challengers: Rep. Rob Wittman in the 1st and Rep. Jen Kiggans in the 2nd.
At the same point in 2024, the partisan composition was relatively split in both districts, with Republican primary voters leading by about 3 points in the 1st District and Democratic primary voters leading by 2 points in the 2nd District.
Statewide, Democratic primary participants outpace Republicans by about 18 points, up from 8 points at the same point in 2024.
Data on pre-election voting is valuable but it does have limits.
Early vote data is compiled by CNN, the Associated Press, and the data firm Catalist, a company that provides data, analytics and other services to Democrats, academics and nonprofit advocacy groups, including insights into who is voting before November.
The number of votes cast so far is a tiny fraction of the roughly 57 million pre-election votes cast in 2022 and an even smaller share of the roughly 112 million votes cast overall in that election but is expected to grow substantially over the next few weeks.
The data so far is also largely limited to mail ballots, as very few states have started significant early in-person voting. In recent years mail voters have been much more Democratic, while early in-person voters have been more evenly split or Republican leaning.

articles.title_orig: A ‘loophole’ in New York’s rape law may have shut the door on criminal charges in the Cornell case. It’s not the first time
articles.title_zh: A ‘loophole’ in New York’s rape law may have shut the door on criminal charges in the Cornell case. It’s not the first time
articles.content_orig:
Resurfaced allegations of a gang rape at a Cornell University fraternity house have renewed outrage over what experts call a legal “loophole” in New York’s – and other states’ – sexual assault laws that can make it nearly impossible for survivors to seek justice if they voluntarily consumed alcohol or drugs before an assault.
At issue in the Cornell case is the fact that the woman, identified only as Jane Doe, says she drank alcohol and accepted drugs the night in 2024 she alleges she was sexually assaulted for hours and advertised as “free p*ssy” by someone in a Chi Phi fraternity member group chat.
The Tompkins County district attorney this week offered many words to describe Doe’s account of how the men assaulted her: disgusting, repugnant, offensive, morally reprehensible.
But he did not call it a crime.
“The young men who engaged in that conduct were morally wrong. It was disgusting, and so she reported that to the police, and the police investigated it. That does not mean – if it’s morally wrong or disgusting or offensive, all those things – it does not mean that the penal law was violated,” prosecutor Matthew Van Houten said on CNN’s “The Situation Room.”
His response has left many asking the same question: How could that be?
The answer, sexual assault survivors and their advocates say, is what’s come to be known as the voluntary intoxication “loophole” or “exclusion,” a gap in the law that exists in about 19 states in the US. It’s one reason countless assaults have gone unprosecuted, experts say, and adds to the overwhelming number of barriers survivors face in seeking justice.
Under one section of New York law , a person is guilty of rape if they engage in sexual contact with someone who is “incapable of consent by reason of being mentally disabled or mentally incapacitated.”
Here’s the “ loophole :” A person is only considered “mentally incapacitated” under the state law if they were temporarily unable to understand or control their actions due to the influence of a narcotic or intoxicating substance administered to them without their consent – or to any other act done to them without their consent.
Jane Doe willingly drank alcohol before arriving at the fraternity house, where members led her upstairs, she stated in a recent state lawsuit. Then, after the men surrounded her and pressured her to take ketamine – a dissociative anesthetic the Drug Enforcement Administration notes has been used to facilitate sexual assault – some of them sexually assaulted her for hours, according to the lawsuit, which seeks damages against seven men allegedly involved.
Cornell University agrees to independent investigation into its handling of alleged sexual assault case
Doe told police she was OK with an initial encounter but said she did not consent to sexual contact later in the night, according to a six-page statement obtained by CNN detailing comments Doe made to investigators in the weeks after the alleged assault. She also described being physically hit.
In addressing Doe’s lawsuit allegations, Van Houten this week referenced her voluntary drug use in explaining the decision not to bring criminal charges, which he said were considered when she first came forward shortly after the incident.
“The facts provided by Jane Doe’s statement do not allege that she was either rendered incapable of controlling her own conduct or that any drug was administered to her without her consent,” he said.
In New York and elsewhere, every legislative session presents a chance to amend the laws around sexual assault. The Cornell rape case has laid bare a systemic failure within the criminal justice system, said Stefan Turkheimer, vice president for public policy at RAINN, an anti-sexual violence organization.
Legislation to remove New York’s voluntary intoxication exclusion has been introduced annually for at least the past eight years without success. Some lawmakers have been pushing for change for even longer.
New York’s law was originally written in the 1990s to address cases where people were “roofied,” or drugged without their knowledge, rendering them unable to consent, New York Assemblyman Jeffrey Dinowitz told CNN.
“Under the current law, somebody being voluntarily intoxicated, which happens all the time, is a virtual get-out-of-jail-free card for somebody who commits a sexual assault,” said Dinowitz, a Democrat. “And that’s just not right.”
In 2019, Dinowitz tried to change that with legislation preventing the use of a victim’s voluntary intoxication as a defense in sex crimes where the victim was incapacitated. He sponsored it again in 2020, 2021, 2022, 2023, 2024, 2025 and 2026. Despite the consistent support of victims’ advocates and other lawmakers, the legislation has never made it to the House for a vote.
What Cornell’s Jane Doe told investigators in 2024 prompts fresh questions
“To me, it’s kind of like there’s a binary choice here,” Dinowitz said. “Either you’re on the side of the survivors of sexual assault or you’re on the side of the people who commit the sexual assaults. And I know where I stand.”
Opponents have raised concerns that it’s difficult to nail down the exact point at which a person becomes too drunk to consent. Others have questioned whether a new law paving the way for more prosecutions would disproportionately impact people of color due to existing biases in the criminal justice system.
The crime of sexual assault can make survivors feel incredibly alone, RAINN’s Turkheimer pointed out. “The way to heal is to come forward, share with others, and find solace and protection and justice in that sharing – but that depends entirely on whether or not it is safe for that person to come forward,” he said.
In the Cornell case, Jane Doe experienced “a textbook reaction to trauma” that likely meant the loss of criminal evidence, her attorney, Thomas Giuffra, told CNN on Thursday. Her “internal processing went from denial, to shame and ultimately acceptance that she had been raped by people that she thought were her friends.”
One of Jane Doe’s roommates couldn’t “really remember her ever kind of citing that she had said yes to anything that occurred,” the roommate said of the first hours after Doe returned home the morning of October 20, 2024, according to documents from a university review of the accusations obtained by The New York Times .
Still, it wasn’t until Doe read an online forum about Greek life shortly after the encounter that “I had ever heard the narrative change that I wasn’t a whore and that I was assaulted,” she told investigators, according to Title IX files compiled as part of the school’s formal process for investigating allegations of sexual harassment and assault.
New documents detail timeline before Cornell’s Jane Doe reported alleged gang rape, NYT reports
Doe “took steps to protect herself and sought STD testing and UTI treatment at Cornell Health on October 22,” her lawyer said, noting Doe told a health care worker she contracted the UTI in a ‘traumatic way.’” But she was not offered expert consultation or a rape kit, which would “likely have revealed DNA which would have been significant information for a criminal investigation,” Giuffra said.
By November 3, 2024, Jane Doe apparently concluded she’d been assaulted at the October party, sending a text to one of the men she would allege was involved: “let’s be clear that 90% of what happened that night was not consensual. i was given more key than i can remember,” she wrote, using a shorthand for ketamine, “and i know that i told u i felt uncomfortable and i didn’t know anyone in the room.”
But by “the time she went for the rape kit on 11/7 all of the DNA evidence was gone,” Giuffra told CNN.
“We really need to think about who we’re protecting and why,” Turkheimer said. “If we are actually trying to encourage survivors to come forward, we have to have people and systems who prioritize their safety.”
Changing these laws state by state has proven difficult – but not impossible.

A customer shops for produce in an H-E-B grocery store in Austin, Texas, on May 11. Brandon Bell/Getty Images hide caption
The Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP) is undergoing a drastic restructuring of its funding model — one that will reduce federal support and require states to shoulder a larger share of the bill.
Historically, the federal government and states have evenly split the food aid program's operational costs, such as paying for state workers and training staff. But starting on Thursday, states will need to cover 75% of that tab while federal funding shrinks by half.
By the federal government's own calculations , the new rule will lead to a $16.9 billion reduction in federal spending for SNAP over the next five years, or $3.4 billion annually.
The Food Research & Action Center, an anti-hunger advocacy group, estimates that states would need to shore up anywhere between $3 million and $670 million to fully offset the loss in federal funding for administrative costs. California, New York, Pennsylvania, Texas and Michigan are expected to be especially hard hit.
Over the past year, states have been rebalancing their budgets to account for the new costs. But they will likely need to tighten their belts even further as more funding changes are on the horizon.
Currently, food benefits are covered entirely by federal dollars. But starting in October 2027, states may have to pay for a portion of the food aid if their error rate — a measure of overpayments and underpayments to SNAP recipients — is at or above 6%.
The Center on Budget and Policy Priorities, a left-leaning think tank, estimates that nearly half of states could each pay $100 million or more if they do not lower their error rates. California and New York could each be on the hook for over $1 billion if they are unable to do so, according to the think tank.
In a report published last year, the Georgetown Center on Poverty and Inequality estimated that these changes together will force states to spend two to three times more to keep the food assistance program running.
These mounting costs will put states in a bind, where they will likely have to find new sources of revenue, cut funding from other programs or further restrict access to SNAP, according to Katie Bergh, a senior policy analyst with the Center on Budget and Policy Priorities.
"And we may see some states decide that they need to withdraw from the program entirely," Bergh says.
The funding changes were triggered by President Trump's signature domestic policy law, the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, which was enacted in July 2025. The White House said the legislation preserves and strengthens the food assistance program, adding that it was "so bloated that it is leaving fewer resources for those who truly need help."
But Bergh says SNAP's previous funding structure served a purpose.
"That essentially ensured that eligible families who were seeking benefits could get them even if they lived in a state that had much higher rates of poverty or a smaller tax base," she says.
The Agriculture Department, which administers SNAP, has not yet responded to a request for comment.
The One Big Beautiful Bill Act also introduced other sweeping changes, adding stricter work requirements and ending food aid eligibility for the small pool of noncitizens who previously qualified.
Since Trump's second term began, the number of people receiving SNAP benefits dropped from 42 million to 36 million, as of June. Most of that decline happened after the One Big Beautiful Bill was signed into law.

Donald Trump defended a series of taxpayer-funded television ads that the administration has spent millions of dollars producing and airing over the last week, saying that the campaign is “promoting the country” — and not himself.
“I’m not running for office,” the president told reporters Wednesday.
“When I’m talking about making America great, making our country great, that’s a countrywide ad,” he said from the Oval Office. “That’s an ad for the spirit of our country.”
The president said that if “somebody” were to tell him that it was “wrong,” he would “gladly pay the money.”
“But these are ads for the country,” he said. “I’m not promoting a candidate or myself. I’m promoting the country.”
The Department of Homeland Security has reportedly tapped as much as $20 million from its budget to produce the ads, and the administration has spent more than $2 million to buy up airtime on national TV networks, where they have already aired hundreds of times.
One of the ads, which appears to be directly lifted from one of the president’s 2024 campaign videos, promotes a “final battle” against “globalists” and “warmongers.” Another video promotes his administration with the song “Love Me” by singer-songwriter JMSN, who has issued a cease-and-desist notice demanding the Trump administration immediately stop using it.
Each of the ads ends with the caption “Paid for by the U.S. Government.”
Legal experts and members of Congress have argued that the ads are a blatantly illegal use of taxpayer dollars that violates ethics laws against the use of public money for partisan political messages and propaganda.
“This is an unlawful and outrageous misuse of public funds,” former White House ethics lawyer and Democracy Defenders Action co-founder Norm Eisen told The Independent this week.
“Federal law forbids using taxpayer dollars for political propaganda, which this clearly is,” he said. “This is yet another corrupt attempt to advance a partisan agenda ahead of the midterm election, paid for by average American taxpayers who are already suffering from high costs caused by this administration’s failed policies.”
The White House has defended the campaign, which it calls “public service announcements.”
“The announcements are very clearly not campaign ads; President Trump is not on the ballot and there is no call to action,” the White House said in a press release last week. “Instead, the announcements are a reminder for Americans to love their country and know why it’s worth defending — at home, at the border, and abroad.”
White House communications director Steven Cheung said: “Don’t let the Fake News get away with their lies about our epic Public Service Announcements that have been running on tv.”
Both Democrats and Republicans have denounced the ads and urged the administration to pull them off the air.
On September 24, a group of congressional Democrats serving on appropriations and finance committees pushed the White House to “immediately take this ad off the air” and “discipline” any federal employees involved.
Public Citizen, a nonprofit consumer advocacy group, has filed a complaint with the federal government accusing the White House of violating the Hatch Act, among other laws.
The Hatch Act prohibits federal employees from engaging in most political activity. The president is largely exempt from the law, but government employees and administration officials who worked on the ads could be in the crosshairs, according to legal experts.
Top Senate Democrats wrote to Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin on Tuesday demanding answers about the agency’s alleged appropriations of public funds to produce the ads, whether any third parties were hired to make them, and whose idea they were in the first place.
“We should not have to remind you that using government funding to create or air political ads like the ones that have been running over the last few days is illegal and a shockingly corrupt misuse of taxpayer dollars,” Senators Patty Murray and Chris Murphy wrote.
The American people deserve answers about how this president is literally stealing their tax dollars to air campaign ads celebrating himself — while doing nothing to help them afford health care or housing,” they added. “These ads need to immediately come off the air, taxpayers need to be paid back for this theft, and everyone responsible needs to be held accountable for this corrupt and illegal propaganda.”
Nonprofit watchdog group Citizens for Responsibility and Ethics in Washington also filed a complaint with Homeland Security’s Office of Inspector General on Wednesday, writing that “this type of spending has no place in federal agencies.”
“The U.S. Treasury is funded by hardworking Americans’ tax dollars and its appropriations must be used for government programs that will improve the lives of those Americans rather than being spent to promote a political campaign agenda that favors those already in power,” the group wrote in a request for an investigation.

articles.title_orig: China-linked hackers posed as former US officials, Anthropic employee to target AI experts
articles.title_zh: China-linked hackers posed as former US officials, Anthropic employee to target AI experts
articles.content_orig:
Chinese hackers impersonated a former senior White House technology official, a former State Department economist and a senior Anthropic employee in attempts to break into the cloud accounts of artificial intelligence policy experts, according to findings from cybersecurity company Proofpoint released Thursday.
The campaigns targeted researchers at think tanks, universities and law firms, using invitations to advise on AI policy and export controls to start conversations. Once recipients responded, the attackers sent links designed to steal their Microsoft login credentials, per the findings.
Among those impersonated were Lynne Parker, a former principal deputy director of the White House Office of Science and Technology Policy, and Heidi Crebo-Rediker, who served as the State Department’s first chief economist.
Proofpoint connected the activity to a group tracked as TA419, describing it as a China-aligned outfit supporting Beijing’s intelligence interests. The report doesn’t say how many people were targeted, whether any accounts were successfully compromised or if the attackers obtained any information.
Beginning July 8, the hackers posed as Parker and then Crebo-Rediker in messages inviting AI experts to join a fictitious “AI Policy Advisory Committee” or contribute to a purported Senate Foreign Relations Committee report on AI export controls and supply chains. Parker’s White House roles included assistant director for AI and founding director of the National AI Initiative Office. Crebo-Rediker, now a Council on Foreign Relations senior fellow, previously worked as the Senate Foreign Relations Committee’s chief of international finance and economics.
After a recipient engaged with the initial messages, the attackers followed up with correspondence that directed targets to a fake OneDrive page used to attempt the account theft.
The group had also used a similar approach in February, impersonating a senior Anthropic employee in an email to an AI policy analyst at a U.S. think tank, Proofpoint said. The subject line read, “Request for Feedback on Military Integration of Claude,” invoking ongoing debate over military use of the company’s AI models. The research did not name the impersonated employee.
The hackers have “consistently shown an interest in defense, national security, energy, international relations, and foreign policy targets, predominantly with a nexus to the U.S. and Japan,” the report says. “The targeting of AI policy experts represents an extension of that remit rather than a departure from it.”
In an email to Nextgov/FCW , Parker confirmed that she learned of the impersonation on July 9, when two recipients contacted her through separate channels to ask whether she had sent the emails. She told them the messages were fraudulent and alerted other colleagues.
“The challenge is that, without knowing who the bad actors are targeting, it’s difficult to reach everyone who might be at risk,” Parker said.
“It is personally troubling to see the trust and relationships I’ve built over my career exploited to deceive others,” she added. “Targeting people in the field can be a way to gain access to valuable information and networks. Protecting America’s AI leadership requires protecting the people and institutions behind it and recognizing that trusted relationships can themselves become a target.”
Crebo-Rediker and Anthropic did not respond to requests for comment. China’s embassy in Washington, D.C., was also contacted. Chinese officials have routinely denied allegations of state-backed hacking and espionage.
The decision to target policy researchers highlights expanding intelligence threats in the global AI race between the U.S., China and other nation-states. Access to experts’ accounts could expose private discussions and professional contacts relevant to decisions about AI’s development, military use and sale abroad. The cyberspies’ approach also illustrates how attackers continue to exploit the dynamics of routine professional exchanges for information-gathering.
The findings also come as AI companies gain an increasingly direct role in Washington’s debate over how to oversee the fast-evolving technology. President Donald Trump met with industry leaders Tuesday to endorse voluntary AI safety commitments . Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei also had dinner with Trump on Sunday.
Proofpoint found that the attackers registered web addresses impersonating the Heritage Foundation, Japan’s defense minister Shinjiro Koizumi and the Japan–Taiwan Exchange Association. Posing as those figures and organizations could help the hackers convince experts that a malicious email is worth their time.
“At the end of the day, humans are our best line of defense,” Don Styer, a former Navy Supply Corps officer and executive vice president for federal services at Consulting Solutions, said in an interview. Attackers can exploit trust through impersonation or seemingly routine requests, he said, adding that foreign adversaries value intelligence they can’t find in public sources and may combine seemingly innocuous details to build a larger picture of a target.
Professional outreach has long been used as an intelligence tool. Nextgov/FCW reported in January that a suspected Chinese spying outfit approached a former senior State Department official last year with an offer to pay for research on U.S. policy toward Venezuela.
The International Consortium of Investigative Journalists reported in June that its reporters received suspicious consulting offers after publishing an investigation into China’s transnational repression. Separately, Britain’s MI5 on Wednesday accused the China General Technology Research Institute of funding academic work to improve Chinese intelligence capabilities. Over 100 U.K.-based academics had contributed to its projects, including research involving AI and cybersecurity, according to the agency, which added that many participants may have been unaware of the institute’s intelligence ties.
The targeting comes amid broader U.S. concerns about Chinese efforts to siphon American AI capabilities. Early last month, the NSA and other agencies accused Chinese developers of conducting large-scale distillation campaigns that use responses from advanced U.S. models to train competing systems.
The attackers revealed in Proofpoint’s findings “will likely continue targeting think tanks and policy experts working on technologies, and in geographies, of particular interest to the Chinese government” and will “likely also continue spoofing the identities of real subject-matter experts,” the company said.

articles.title_orig: Egg prices have tumbled since Trump returned to office. Here's why
articles.title_zh: Egg prices have tumbled since Trump returned to office. Here's why
articles.content_orig:
Eggs are given out for free in front of Brown Butter Craft Bar & Kitchen in New York City on March 21, 2025. The cost of a dozen eggs reached a record high of $6.23 that month. Michael M. Santiago/Getty Images hide caption
President Trump has repeatedly boasted about bringing down egg prices during his second term. He's often blamed former President Joe Biden for the recent high costs American consumers were paying for the dietary staple, claiming it was his return to office that finally put an end to runaway egg prices.
It's true that the price of eggs has declined by more than half over the course of Trump's second term. According to federal data , the average cost of a dozen eggs when he took office in January 2025 was $4.95, while the typical price this August was just $2.27.
But the reasons why egg prices have plunged so far in that time are complicated, and agriculture industry experts say the administration has taken other actions that have made it harder for farms to turn a profit.
Perhaps the single most significant factor affecting egg prices in the past five years has little to do with policy. Avian flu wiped out flocks across the U.S. and ate into domestic egg supplies, causing retail prices to take off. Prices went down again as flocks recovered.
"That's been the big factor, and it's overwhelming everything else," said Michael Walden, an emeritus professor of economics at North Carolina State University.
The Trump administration has helped farmers beef up biosecurity measures to protect their flocks, and Walden also noted that the U.S. Department of Agriculture tried to cut red tape for egg farmers. But he said Trump's tariffs on foreign trading partners and the war with Iran have made life harder for farmers by driving up their operating costs for necessities like diesel .
"While the federal government has tried to loosen some regulations on farmers to reduce costs, the benefits there have been far outweighed by the negatives," he said.
Now, as the midterm elections approach, Trump and his fellow Republicans continue to grapple with voters' concerns about affordability — in particular, the cost of food.
Beginning in early 2022, the U.S. began experiencing its largest outbreak of highly pathogenic avian influenza (HPAI), or avian flu, in years. It resulted in the deaths of millions of egg-laying hens that year, and prices rose in the ensuing months.
A similar pattern repeated in late 2024 and early 2025, when another wave of avian flu tore through U.S. farms. According to the USDA's Economic Research Service , nearly 51 million egg-laying hens died or were euthanized between October 2024 and March 2025 alone.
A smaller flock was left to lay eggs, causing prices to surge. The cost of a dozen eggs reached a record high of $6.23 in March 2025, just two months into Trump's second term.
Consumers felt the price increase acutely. Agriculture industry experts say that's because eggs are what economists call an inelastic product, meaning demand for eggs doesn't change much when the cost goes up.
Emily Metz, president and CEO of the American Egg Board, an industry marketing group, says that's because eggs hold an indispensable place in the American diet.
"Not only are they a center of the plate item, not only do people eat them by themselves, but people also use them in baked goods, use them in drinks to froth and whip things up," she said. "They use them in all sorts of recipes and in different ways."
This past winter proved a less severe period for avian flu on U.S. farms, and farmers were able to rebuild their flocks , helping to calm last year's record prices.
In February of last year, after the worst of the avian flu outbreak, Agriculture Secretary Brooke Rollins announced up to $1 billion to combat the disease that had swept through the nation's flocks.
It included up to $500 million to help farms enhance biosecurity protections , which include things like hygiene protocols and safeguards against wildlife, supplementing what many producers had already been doing. (The USDA had conducted biosecurity assessments at more than 900 farms as of June 2025.) As much as $400 million was set aside to pay farmers who've had to cull their flocks or destroy eggs in response to a potential infection, and the amount of compensation they could receive per bird went up .
Metz of the American Egg Board said farmers always work closely with the USDA during avian flu outbreaks, and that the plan from Rollins helped, too. But it's also true that last year's avian flu season was simply much milder.
"I think those initiatives have advanced, but we've also benefitted in the industry because bird flu is very cyclical," Metz said. "It follows the wild bird population, and so we haven't had bird flu in the environment in the same way this year that we had last year."
The USDA also said last year that it would explore ways to increase egg imports — and imports did spike. U.S. egg imports in 2025 reached 121 million dozen-equivalent, way up from the 29.8 million dozen-equivalent imported the previous year .
Mark Jordan, executive director of LEAP Market Analytics, a consulting firm specializing in animal protein markets, said that though the uptick in imports was a positive step toward replenishing the domestic supply devastated by avian flu, it had a relatively modest impact on the U.S. poultry industry, which produces around 90 billion eggs per year. "That's not nothing, but that's a small impact," he said.
Jordan said ultimately the turnaround in egg prices came from how well farms were protected from infection — and how serious that wave of illness was. "I'd say 90-95% of the impact that we've seen in terms of prices coming down has just been some measure of biosecurity success and some measure of, you know, luck," he said.
Also last year, the Justice Department along with 17 states settled a case of alleged price-fixing against three major egg producers — Cal-Maine Foods, Hickman's Egg Ranch and Versova. Prosecutors alleged that coordination among the companies pushed egg prices even higher in recent years.
Even as the Trump administration has responded to the avian flu, it has also imposed tariffs on foreign trading partners and gone to war with Iran — both of which have surged operational costs for U.S. farmers, industry experts said.
Poultry farmers have faced "pretty stiff inflationary pressures from corn and soybean meal" to feed their flocks, Jordan said, while Metz with the American Egg Board noted that others who grow crops to feed their birds have encountered higher fertilizer costs. Transportation prices have shot up due to higher energy prices.
And egg producers have also seen higher costs for packaging, including cardboard and other corrugated materials that have been affected by U.S. trade negotiations with Canada, Metz said.
"There's a lot of inputs that go into a farm that people don't realize beyond just the animal itself, and all of those inputs have increased in cost pretty significantly over the last several years," she said.
That's put pressure not just on egg producers, but the food industry writ large, pushing up overall grocery prices for U.S. consumers. Federal data showed that grocery prices in August were up 2.2% in a year, even as egg prices declined 23% in the same period.

articles.title_orig: Bipartisan Senate duo drops new data center bills
articles.title_zh: Bipartisan Senate duo drops new data center bills
articles.content_orig:
Senate Democrats on Wednesday blocked a GOP-led bill to combat rising energy costs driven by the data center boom, thwarting a last-ditch effort by Republicans to show they are taking voter concerns about affordability seriously.
Even though the bill only recommends states take action and does not mandate lower prices for consumers, the bill’s failure deprives Republicans of an opportunity to counter attacks that they haven’t done enough to tackle high prices ahead of the midterms. It deals a setback to one vulnerable Republican senator in particular: Ohio’s Jon Husted, who led the charge for passage of the bill after being hammered on the issue in his race, one of the most competitive Senate battlegrounds.
Now, senators are expected to soon leave Washington and not return until after the midterms as a number of Senate Republicans have expressed concern that their party has not done enough to address the high cost of living in the run-up to a critical election where control of Congress is at stake.
The vote also opens Democrats up to criticism for blocking the bill, which passed the House earlier this month with widespread bipartisan support.
The measure — known as the “Ratepayer Protection Act” — was blocked on a 57 to 43 vote with only four Democrats voting with Republicans.
Senate Democrats said ahead of the vote that they opposed the bill because it did not go far enough. The bill requires state regulators to “consider” adopting a proposed federal standard that would require data center companies to cover their costs to the energy grid, rather than passing it off to consumers. Democrats said the language was weak and lacked enforcement mechanisms.
“Here we need some real action on data centers and what does the Republican senator from Ohio come up with? Something that is optional,” Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer said on the floor Tuesday, as Democrats vowed to seek passage of more robust measures.
The vote, in the Senate’s final days in Washington before the midterms, highlights the fight between both parties as they scramble to show voters they’re better equipped to tackle the high cost of living. It also comes as the expansion of data centers powered by AI has sparked concern among Americans.
Republicans criticized Democrats ahead of the vote for their opposition, saying this was the best chance to take action on the issue.
“This is the bill that gives us a chance to prove to the American people that we’re for lower electricity prices and holding data centers accountable. So the only way that this happen is if this bill passes,” Husted said. “This bill is the only game in town.”
Communities fighting against the buildings that power AI
But Democrats brushed off concerns the optics of their opposition could backfire.
“If ratepayers read this (bill) and see that it’s a name that says ratepayer protection and provides no relief in rates, they’ll rightly be angry. They can see something that’s not on the level,” said Sen. Peter Welch of Vermont. “You know, I think voters see this for what it is: as kind of a political maneuver at the 11th hour.”
Husted had taken on the mission of passing the bill amid a critical and highly competitive Senate race as Republicans fight to retain their Senate majority.
Data centers have become a flashpoint in his race against Democrat and former Sen. Sherrod Brown, as communities in the Buckeye state have experienced firsthand the rapid development of AI processing facilities. In his role as lieutenant governor and as a senator, Husted has applauded the economic boom that the centers can bring but has also pushed to approve the “Ratepayer Protection Act” as a way to attempt to neutralize potential backlash.
It was Husted who pushed party leaders to return to Washington this week to vote on the bill after leaders had weighed an early exit ahead of the midterms. Multiple sources told CNN that Husted implored his colleagues not to head home early without at least attempting the vote to send a message that Republicans were doing something on the issue of affordability.
Back in Ohio, Brown has cut several ads attacking Husted on the centers. And in August, Senate Republicans’ campaign committee, the National Republican Senatorial Committee, sent an internal memo warning “more than any other thing in this race, data centers are the anchor hanging around Husted’s neck.”
“This has become a sleeper issue for the entire cycle,” the NRSC wrote.
Husted’s campaign spokesperson Amy Natoce accused Democrats of playing politics by blocking the bill.
“The House overwhelmingly passed Sen. Husted’s bipartisan legislation requiring data center companies to pay for the power they use, but Senate Democrats blocked it. Sherrod Brown and his friends would rather play politics and stick Ohio families with higher electric bills than pass a commonsense solution,” she said.
In a statement, Lauren Chou, a Brown campaign spokesperson, said, “Jon Husted led the charge to bring data centers to Ohio, forcing Ohioans to pay thousands more in higher electric bills and giving giant out-of-state corporations billions of dollars in out-of-control tax breaks.”
“Ohioans should get to decide if data centers are built in their communities and should never be forced to subsidize the electricity costs of big corporations,” Chou said.
Still, in the Senate’s last days of work, some Republicans have suggested that the party could be doing more to tackle affordability.
“My view is that people would love some relief in the price of their gas. They would love some relief in the price of their health care. They would love some rights vis a vis these data centers. If it were me, I’d make those thing priorities,” Missouri Republican Sen. Josh Hawley said.
Sen. John Kennedy, a Republican from Louisiana, bemoaned that the party is facing economic headwinds amid the fight to keep the House and Senate in the midterms.
“I mean you don’t have to be a senior at Cal Tech to understand that people are angry about the cost of living, and they’re confused about Iran and the two are inextricably linked,” Kennedy said last week.

American officials increasingly believe China is unlikely to attack Taiwan before 2028, despite President Xi Jinping ordering his military to be able to seize the island by force by 2027, according to sources familiar with Washington's assessments.
China's military readiness has been hampered by Xi's sweeping anti-corruption purge, while Beijing may also want to see the outcome of Taiwan's 2028 presidential election before deciding its next move, two serving US officials, a former official and another person familiar with the matter said.
But the risk of military action could rise significantly if Taiwan's ruling Democratic Progressive Party wins an unprecedented fourth consecutive presidential term, particularly if President Lai Ching-te is reelected.
"If that happens, I think 2028 becomes pretty sporty," one US official said.
Lai and the DPP champion Taiwan's separate identity, angering Beijing, which considers the self-governed island part of its territory. Taiwan rejects China's sovereignty claims and says its people can decide its future.
The assessment marks a shift from concerns about 2027, when Xi ordered the People's Liberation Army to be capable of taking Taiwan by force. US officials have long viewed the date, which marks the PLA's centenary, as a military readiness target rather than a firm invasion deadline.
Beijing has never publicly acknowledged plans to attack Taiwan in 2027 and continues to say it favors peaceful "reunification," while refusing to renounce the use of force.
US intelligence agencies have also previously identified signs of caution. In their annual threat assessment in March, they said Beijing had no fixed timeline for invading Taiwan and continued to prefer taking control of the island without war if possible.
The Pentagon declined to comment. The Chinese Embassy in Washington and Taiwan's representative office did not immediately respond to requests for comment.
Washington remains Taipei's primary global benefactor and defense vendor despite lacking official diplomatic relations, though American officials provided varying views regarding how heavily Beijing might weigh the outcome of the 2028 U.S. presidential election when evaluating potential military maneuvers.
Although three sources said Chinese strategists might want to gauge the U.S. political outcome—especially amid waning public enthusiasm in America for overseas military engagements—the primary U.S. official emphasized that Beijing considers both Democratic and Republican parties essentially unified in their firm backing of Taiwan.
While Chinese leadership might prefer a certain outcome in the 2028 American vote, "it doesn't become as decisive a factor in my opinion, as it might have been 15 years ago," the official said.
President Donald Trump has consistently minimized the threat of an imminent Chinese assault on Taiwan under his watch, claiming publicly last year that Xi personally assured him Beijing would abstain from invading while he remained in power.
Trump offered brief remarks on Taiwan after his bilateral meeting with Xi in Washington last week, confirming only that Taiwan came up during their exchange and that Xi fully understood his stance.
Beijing repeatedly describes Taiwan as its paramount political priority and a non-negotiable matter touching upon sovereign integrity.
China has persistently demanded a complete halt to American military aid to Taiwan. Following his May visit to Beijing, Trump suspended approval of an approximate $14 billion arms deal, characterizing the military assistance package as a leverage tool or "negotiating chip."
Decades of American policy have concentrated on bolstering Taiwan's defensive capacity, enabling the island to withstand an initial Chinese offensive until Washington and partner nations can intervene defensively.
Chinese leader Xi has not formally abandoned his directive ordering the People's Liberation Army to possess full operational capability to seize Taiwan by force next year, officials noted.
However, the armed forces failed to meet their target operational benchmarks over the past year because Beijing's extensive anti-corruption sweep disrupted progress, sources explained.
Since assuming power in 2012, Xi has spearheaded an uncompromising campaign targeting corruption and party disloyalty. Millions of bureaucrats across China's state apparatus have faced investigation, resulting in the downfall and removal of numerous high-ranking party leaders, officials, and commanders.
Recently, the People's Liberation Army became a primary focus of this internal purge. A wave of high-level inquiries and dismissals leaves only two active members on the once seven-person Central Military Commission, including Xi, who remains chair.
Chinese military maneuvers last year were visibly smaller in scale and less aggressive than in previous periods, according to the U.S. official. Although drills expanded somewhat this year, the official indicated top Chinese military commanders remained privately dissatisfied with force readiness levels.
The official noted Beijing appears to have extracted critical insights from recent conflicts in Iran and Ukraine, realizing that an invasion requires immediate, overwhelming success to prevent becoming entangled in an exhausting, prolonged war of attrition.
Significant operational hurdles remain unaddressed.
"There are way too many pieces that aren't quite in place yet for what would be the most difficult military operation any military has attempted probably since the Allied invasion of Normandy," the official said.

Memory giant Micron ( MU ) reported its fourth quarter earnings after the bell on Wednesday, beating Wall Street's expectations on the top and bottom lines and offering a better-than-anticipated Q1 outlook.
For the quarter, Micron reported earnings per share of $33.42 on revenue of $54.23 billion. Analysts were looking for EPS of $31.83 and revenue of $51.49 billion, according to Bloomberg analyst consensus estimates.
The company saw EPS of $3.03 and revenue of $11.31 billion in the same quarter last year.
For the second quarter, Micron is projecting revenue of between $60 billon and $63 billion; analysts were calling for $56.77 billion.
Micron's fortunes , along with those of fellow memory chip producers Samsung ( 005930.KS ) and SK Hynix ( SKHY ), have soared amid sky-high demand driven by the global AI build-out.
Data centers require massive amounts of DRAM , used in high-bandwidth memory that goes into AI processors, including graphics processing units (GPUs), as well as ultra-fast flash storage. Micron produces both of those.
That's helped propel the company's stock price to staggering heights, with shares rising roughly 275% year to date and 550% over the past 12 months as of Wednesday.
Micron is also making big bets on its future growth. In August, the company announced that it would invest up to $10 billion over the next 10 years to build out a "long-horizon premier research institution" in Boise, Idaho.
While the AI boom has been a boon for memory makers, it's taking a toll on other sectors of the tech industry.
Consumer electronics manufacturers have raised prices on their devices to offset the rising cost of memory and storage chips. Most recently, Apple ( AAPL ) raised the prices of its iPhone 18 Pro line by $100 compared with its iPhone 17 Pro .
While the price increases have cut into the number of devices manufacturers are selling, the higher price tags have offset much of the negative impact on their bottom lines

articles.title_zh: Star power, pitching and more takeaways from Cubs-Padres Wild Card Series
articles.content_orig:
SAN DIEGO -- The Padres made sure this year was different.
The 2025 iteration of this National League Wild Card Series in Chicago left a sour taste in San Diego’s mouth, and rightfully so. An already struggling lineup flatlined. There were virtually no big moments. They didn’t have a raucous Petco Park behind them.
San Diego flipped the script completely, cruising through a dominant -- and very loud -- two nights to sweep the Cubs in the NL Wild Card Series, capped by a 4-1 win in Wednesday’s Game 2. The Padres will now advance to the Division Series to face the No. 1 seeded Brewers, who won an MLB-best 103 games during the regular season. Game 1 is on Saturday in Milwaukee.
“We’re playing our best baseball at the right time,” said Padres first baseman Ty France. “We’re looking forward to continuing it.”
Here are some takeaways from the Padres' sweep:
1. The Padres' stars outshined the Cubs’ stars
For the Cubs, the result is quite the disappointment. They came into the series boasting a league-best offense led by likely NL MVP Pete Crow-Armstrong and postseason stalwart Alex Bregman. The Padres held both in check throughout the series, while San Diego’s dynamic duo of Fernando Tatis Jr. and Manny Machado took over -- along with the rest of the Padres’ lineup.
Tatis and Machado were the stars of San Diego’s 8-0 rout in Game 1 -- each belting a home run in the overwhelming win. Xander Bogaerts and Jackson Merrill combined for eight hits across the pair of victories.
On the other side, Crow-Armstrong and Bregman combined to go 0-for-15 in the two games with eight strikeouts between them.
“I’m just pretty disappointed in myself,” Crow-Armstrong said. “You can look at the scoreboard. You can look at the stat sheet. Wherever you get your numbers from. It’s clear to see that I didn’t contribute.”
2. The San Diego bullpen was built for this
Hear me out: If you’re the Cubs -- and you need to win a game to keep your season alive -- probably not a great idea to fall behind the Padres early at Petco Park, with the stable of arms they have looming in the bullpen.
The San Diego bullpen was built precisely with this kind of moment in mind. And the Padres executed their plan to perfection on Wednesday.
“In the postseason, you’ve got to get a lot of great hitters out,” said general manager A.J. Preller. “You’ve got to have a lot of answers in that bullpen.”
With Preller as the architect, the Padres always do. Bradgley Rodriguez, Jason Adam, Adrian Morejon and Mason Miller combined for 5 2/3 scoreless innings on Wednesday. Really, the series was probably over when Michael King covered seven dominant innings in Game 1, preserving that entire ‘pen for a night like this one.
“King was the key to this whole series, his ability to go seven,” said pitching coach Ruben Niebla. “Going into today it was like: We know where we’re at. … We knew we had six innings we could cover. It worked out to perfection.”
3. The Cubs’ lineup went quiet overall
A deep run into October was going to require the Cubs’ high-scoring offense to deliver in the manner it did in the regular season. The North Siders led the Majors in runs scored, walks, slugging percentage and OPS, while also leading the NL in homers.
In the two losses in San Diego, Chicago’s lineup went dark beyond just Crow-Armstrong and Bregman. As a whole, the unit hit .129 (8-for-62) with just one run scored.
“We didn’t score runs,” said Nico Hoerner, whose RBI single in the fourth represented the lone breakthrough in the series. “We have a great lineup. I think we were prepared. I think that’s kind of the harsh reality of a three-game series to end the season, right? I’m sure there were plenty of two-game stretches during the season we didn’t produce.
“They executed at a really high level. Obviously, their bullpen is incredibly talented and they showed that tonight.”
4. Petco Park is an October force
Machado is a veteran of eight postseasons. He’s seen his share of rabid playoff crowds (including a few in Milwaukee, where the Padres are headed next).
This week, Machado said, was on another level.
“I’ve never seen anything like it,” he said. “That was huge.”
It’s going to be awfully tough to beat the Padres in San Diego this postseason. No doubt, the Padres would love to win a pair in Milwaukee. But realistically, if they can earn a split this weekend, they’ll like their chances heading back home for Games 3 and 4.
